world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Ross, Malcolm 2002. 'Takia', in Lynch, Ross & Crowley (eds.) The Oceanic Languages; also SIL PNG Takia Organised Phonology Data (sil.org 403).

new_statements.quote: Primary stress placement in Takia is unusual in that it is related to vowel height. Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'. However, it occurs on an earlier syllable if that syllable's vowel is lower than the vowel(s) of any succeeding syllables: nanu-n ['nanun] child-3SG 'her/his child'; ŋa-sol ['ŋasol] 1SG-flee 'I fled'.
new_statements.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Takia. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages, 216-248. Richmond: Curzon.
new_statements.locator: §1.3 'Stress and syllabification', p. 218 (archive.org PDF p. 235); secondary stress pp. 218-220; clitics/formative p. 221
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default final stress within the phonological word (root plus affixes), overridden by vowel height: primary stress goes to the leftmost syllable whose vowel is strictly lower (more sonorous: a > e,o > i,u) than the vowels of every following syllable; with equal or rising vowel height the last syllable wins (ta'man, u'sol, ifu'no) while a lower earlier vowel attracts it ('nanun, 'ŋasol). Many pre-tonic [i]/[u] are non-lexical inserted vowels (lexical /krŋen/ -> [kiri'ŋen]) and do not affect placement; Ross notes stress is 'redundant' (predictable) and marks it only for readability. Not syllable-weight-based in the usual sense: the 'weight' is vowel sonority, so a fixed-final-with-sonority-override reading is equally defensible.
new_statements.secondary_stress: After the primary ('part B'): if two or three syllables follow, a secondary stress falls on the second syllable after the primary regardless of vowel (kanaorig [ka.'na.o.ˌrig] 'earthquake'), 'often hardly perceptible'. Before the primary ('part A'): with two or more preceding syllables, secondary stress falls on any (C)VC syllable or any syllable with /a/, otherwise on every second syllable leftward from the primary (i-fn-o [ˌi.fu.'no]; kumatiao [ku.ˌma.ti.'a.o]); /a/ syllables in part A are always secondarily stressed, producing adjacent stressed syllables (tama-n [ˌta.'man]), optionally reduced in words of three or more syllables; with three or more /a/ syllables in a row one unpredictably loses its stress and vowel (wananan [ˌwa.ˌna.'nan] ~ [ˌwan.'nan]). Unstressed vowels may reduce to [ə].
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics and the derivational formative /-a-/ are never stressed and are excluded from stress assignment (p. 221: /ai-a-n/ 'hipbone' ['ayan] keeps stress on the initial vowel); an optional (a) in some pronoun forms is 'treated as non-existent for stress assignment purposes' (p. 222); a small class of exceptions arises from vowel prothesis before initial /r/ (p. 219). Ross states the 2002 account differs 'significantly' from his 1995 CAD sketch and that the trigger-vowel/stress relationship claimed there is irrelevant ('Waters, contra Ross 1995').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = root + affixes, excluding clitics (phrase-attached) and the formative. Data are from the coastal dialect recorded at Rigen village, south Karkar Island, 1987-88 (consultant Mait Kilil); Ross says the phonology is the same in all dialects apart from the inland /l/-/r/ merger, but phonetic realisation and part-A syllabification vary between dialects and tokens. The example lists in the quote are tabular in the original (form / phonetic / gloss / translation columns) and have been run together with semicolons.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 describes the coastal Takia dialect of Rigen village (southern Karkar Island), stating the phonology is otherwise uniform across dialects (inland dialects merge /l/ and /r/). Glottolog taki1248 has no dialect glottocodes; the mainland 'Megiar/Sarang' varieties listed under Takia in the hh bibliography are not covered by the stress description. The SIL OPD (Waters 1992) covers Karkar and Bagabag with no dialect split for phonology.

Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'. sources.locator: §1.3 'Stress and syllabification', p. 218 (archive.org PDF p. 235); secondary stress pp. 218-220; clitics/formative p. 221
sources.note: Primary stress falls by default on the final syllable of the phonological word (root+affixes, not clitics), but moves to an earlier syllable whose vowel is lower than all following vowels; detailed secondary-stress rules for the syllables before ('part A') and after ('part B') the primary stress; clitics and the formative -a- are never stressed. Ross says this account is 'significantly different from the one in Ross (1995)'.
No stress features (14A-17A) coded for Takia.
